target_customer: Game studios, from indie to large mobile publishers, that need multiplayer, social and live operations backend
problem: Studios keep rebuilding the same scalable backend features such as accounts, matchmaking, leaderboards and live ops instead of focusing on the game.
business_model: Open source game server with paid managed hosting (Heroic Cloud) and commercial products (Hiro, Satori), per product descriptions
product_category: Game backend and live operations infrastructure

founders.name: Chris Molozian
education: Queen Mary, University of London (per company 10 year letter, met co-founders there)
founders.background_notes: Described as software engineer and tinkerer on distributed systems; worked as a server engineer before founding.

founders.name: Mo Firouz
education: Queen Mary, University of London (per company 10 year letter)
founders.background_notes: Company letter says the three worked as server engineers before founding; employers not named.

founders.name: Andrei Mihu
education: Queen Mary, University of London (per company 10 year letter)
founders.background_notes: Scalable systems and high availability design per YC page.

technical_complexity.rationale: A distributed, real-time game server with persistence and social features had to scale to many concurrent players, and later powered migrations such as a large platform's games, which is hard for a three person team.

defensibility.rationale: Open source adoption and deep integration into live games create switching costs, but the core server is open source so anyone can fork it.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: The CEO letter says Amazon later shut down its GameTech service and Heroic Labs migrated about 95 percent of its clients; no incumbent copied or bought the company.

market_need_then: The CEO letter says developers were rebuilding backend technology that should already exist. Other backend providers (for example Parse, shut down in 2016) left gaps that the team cited when moving from SaaS to open source in 2017.

branding.name_origin: Heroic: studios are seen as heroes fighting technical complexity, time pressure and scalability. Nakama is a Japanese word for friends as close as family, chosen to fit the origin story (company 10 year letter).
branding.domain_note: Uses heroiclabs.com; no acquisition history found.

identity.logo: Not described by any source opened

branding.brand_signature: Nakama, the open source social server, with a Japanese friendship name
branding.community_and_virality: Nakama GitHub stars grew from about one thousand in 2018 to over ten thousand by 2025 per an interview; sponsors Godot and Defold development.

brand_strength.rationale: Strong developer community presence and open source sponsorships, and the product brand Nakama is better known than the company name, but no wider consumer brand effect.

pivots.to: Open source Nakama server with paid hosting and add-on products
pivots.why: Company letter says it moved from SaaS to open source and the earlier shutdown of Parse prompted the change

outcome_analysis: Heroic Labs stayed bootstrapped and founder led per its 10 year letter, found traction after open sourcing Nakama in 2017, won large client migrations, and reports about one million developers and hundreds of millions of installs. It grew through capital efficiency and a successful pivot to open source with paid products rather than venture rounds.
notes: Company letter states it stayed bootstrapped, so no priced rounds are recorded; aggregators list a $120K YC seed in August 2015 (YC standard deal, not a round) and one directory lists $10M raised and a Caplight headline lists a $16M Series A, both unverified and likely wrong. Outcome search found no acquisition, layoffs or shutdown. Founders' prior employers are not named in sources opened. Competitor search found no sources dated near 2015 (Nakama itself launched publicly in 2017) so the list is empty. Founding year: YC page says 2014, one directory says 2013.
